INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE
Amici are 189 members of the United States Congress
whose constituents include lawful gun owners, hunters,
and sportsmen, as well as individuals and communities
affected by gun violence. 1  Many represent communities
that have experienced mass shootings involving assault
weapons and who continue to live with the deaths, injuries,
grief, and lasting effects those attacks leave behind.  Amici
must answer to all of these constituencies while making
difficult legislative judgments that respect constitutional
rights and confront the devastating consequences of gun
violence.
Amici regularly confront questions of firearms
policy in their legislative capacities.  Through hearings,
investigations, constituent engagement, and debate, they
assess evidence, draw regulatory lines, and accommodate
competing concerns.  They must then decide whether
legislative action is warranted and what form it should
take—and answer to their constituents for the choices
they make.
Congress has repeatedly undertaken that work with
respect to assault weapons, most notably in enacting
the Federal Assault Weapons Ban after years of
hearings and deliberation.  That experience gives amici
a particular perspective on the judgments involved in
regulating assault weapons, why those judgments belong
1. Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, amici state that no

2
to legislatures, and the consequences of removing them
from the democratic process.
Amici submit this brief to explain why, where the
Second Amendment permits regulation, decisions about
its scope, design, and revision properly belong to elected
legislatures—and why preserving that responsibility is
essential to representative government.
The names of individual amici are listed in the
Appendix to this brief.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Our Constitution does more than constrain
government; it also assigns responsibility for governing.
Although the Second Amendment imposes constitutional
limits on firearms regulation, within those limits,
decisions about whether and how to regulate assault
weapons properly belong to federal, state, and local
lawmakers.  The judiciary’s role is to interpret and
enforce those constitutional limits, not to choose among
the policy options that remain available.  That allocation
of responsibility reflects a fundamental feature of
representative government: lawmakers are uniquely
situated to make policy judgments—they are accountable
to the people affected and possess the institutional tools
to address complex policy questions.  Their responsibility
is to hear competing voices, assess evidence that is often
incomplete or contested, make predictive judgments, and
answer to voters for both action and inaction.  Lawmakers
can also revisit their decisions as technology, evidence,
and experience evolve.

3
Congress’s experience with the Federal Assault
Weapons Ban shows what that responsibility looks like
in practice, and why preserving it is important to our
constitutional system.  Congress spent years examining
assault weapons, hearing from competing constituencies,
and debating whether and how a federal restriction should
be drawn.  The resulting statute reflected a series of
policy judgments, including which weapons and features
to regulate, how to treat existing lawful owners, what
exceptions to recognize, and whether the federal regime
should continue indefinitely.  Congress then had the
benefit of evidence generated while the Ban was in force—
evidence both of its meaningful effects and of limitations
in the law’s design.
To be clear, courts retain the responsibility to enforce
the Second Amendment’s limits, but that is not the same
as making the policy judgments the Constitution leaves
open.  A categorical rule foreclosing prohibitions on the
semiautomatic rifles at issue, as Petitioners urge, would
remove that regulatory option from Congress, the States,
and local governments, even as weapons, evidence, and
experience continue to change.  The Constitution protects
individual rights while entrusting elected lawmakers with
the policy judgments that remain within constitutional
bounds.  Amici therefore urge the Court to reject the
categorical prohibition Petitioners seek and affirm the
judgments below, preserving the authority of elected
lawmakers to determine whether and how to regulate
assault weapons consistent with the Second Amendment.

4
ARGUMENT
I.  WITHIN CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITS, ASSAULT-
WEAPONS POLICY BELONGS TO LAWMAKERS,
NOT COURTS
Within the limits imposed by the Second Amendment,
the Constitution entrusts decisions about whether and
h o w  to  r e gul a te  fir e arm s  to  e l e c te d  l a wm ak e rs .   Th a t
allocation of responsibility reflects the respective roles
of courts and lawmakers, as well as the distinctive
features of representative government.  Lawmakers are
accountable to the people affected by their decisions,
possess institutional tools suited to complex policy
judgments, and can revisit those judgments as evidence
and experience evolve.
A.  Lawmakers have broad authority to address gun
violence, subject to the Second Amendment’s
limits.
Lawmakers have broad authority to address public
safety, subject to constitutional constraints, including
those imposed by the Second Amendment.  As this Court
recognized in District of Columbia v. Heller , the right to
keep and bear arms is “not unlimited,” 554 U.S. 570, 626
(2008), and governments retain a “variety of tools” for
addressing gun violence, id. at 636.  Within those bounds,
choosing which tools to use is a legislative responsibility.
That authority is not confined to the precise
regulatory choices of earlier generations.  New York State
Rifle & Pistol Ass’n, Inc. v. Bruen recognized that “cases
implicating unprecedented societal concerns or dramatic

5
technological changes may require a more nuanced
approach,” because “[t]he regulatory challenges posed
by firearms today are not always the same as those that
preoccupied the Founders in 1791 or the Reconstruction
generation in 1868.”  597 U.S. 1, 27 (2022).  The historical
inquiry is “neither a regulatory straightjacket nor a
regulatory blank check.”  Id. at 30.  And in United
States v. Rahimi , the Court emphasized that its Second
Amendment precedents “were not meant to suggest a
law trapped in amber.”  602 U.S. 680, 691 (2024).  Rather,
“the Second Amendment permits more than just those
regulations identical to ones that could be found in 1791.”
Id. at 691–92.  A modern law must “comport with the
principles underlying the Second Amendment, but need
not be a ‘dead ringer’ or ‘historical twin’” of an earlier
enactment.  Id. at 692.
Justice Barrett’s concurrence in Rahimi expressed
the institutional concern with demanding greater
historical specificity: “[h]istorical regulations reveal a
principle, not a mold.”  Id. at 740 (Barrett, J., concurring).
An approach requiring overly specific historical analogues
would wrongly assume that earlier legislatures had
“maximally exercised their power to regulate,” effectively
adopting a “‘use it or lose it’ view of legislative authority.”
Id. at 739–40.
Amici take seriously their responsibility to legislate
consistently with the Second Amendment.  But its
constitutional limits do not eliminate the judgments that
remain for lawmakers to make.  Where regulation is
permissible, lawmakers must still determine whether
action is warranted and what form it should take.

6
B.  The Constitution assigns policy judgments
about public safety to Congress and the States,
not courts.
“Under the system of government created by our
Constitution, it is up to legislatures, not courts, to decide on
the wisdom and utility of legislation.”  Ferguson v. Skrupa,
372 U.S. 726, 729 (1963).  That division of responsibility
reflects a basic feature of representative government:
crafting workable policies requires “balancing interests
and often demands compromise,” a task entrusted to
elected lawmakers.  Hernandez v. Mesa , 589 U.S. 93,
100 (2020).  As this Court has recognized, Congress
has the “constitutional power” to “regulate interstate
commerce,” and Congress may exercise such power so
“that the public health and safety might be advanced.”
United States v. Walsh , 331 U.S. 432, 434 (1947).  State
legislatures likewise possess broad authority over public
health and safety under their traditional police powers.
See Medtronic, Inc. v. Lohr , 518 U.S. 470, 475 (1996)
(recognizing that States have “great latitude under their
police powers” to protect the health and safety of their
citizens).  This Court has described the suppression of
violent crime as “the prime object of the States’ police
power.”  United States v. Morrison , 529 U.S. 598, 615
(2000); see also Barnes v. Glen Theatre, Inc., 501 U.S. 560,
569 (1991) (“The traditional police power of the States is
defined as the authority to provide for the public health,
safety, and morals”).  That authority dates to the earliest
days of the Republic, when state legislatures exercised
the “authority to adopt such regulations of police, as may
be dictated by the safety of the people.”  State v. Reid , 1
Ala. 612, 616 (1840).  Local governments, including Cook
County, in turn exercise public-safety authority conferred
by state law.

7
Bruen keeps that authority where the Constitution
puts it—with lawmakers like amici, not judges.  It rejected
means-ends scrutiny precisely because that approach
invited judges to subjectively weigh policy considerations
that lawmakers are better equipped to weigh, substituting
judicial judgment for the constitutional boundary supplied
by text and history.  See 597 U.S. at 23–25.  As the Fourth
Circuit put it, “lower courts are duty bound to apply the
terms of the balance enshrined in the Constitution’s text,
not to dictate such terms themselves.”  Bianchi v. Brown,
111 F .4th 438, 472 (4th Cir. 2024) (en banc).  Bruen forbids
judges from acting as policymakers; it does not strip
legislators of that role.  Where the Second Amendment
leaves room for regulation, this Court has “no authority
to second-guess” the choices amici and their colleagues
make amongst various permissible options.  Husted v. A.
Philip Randolph Inst., 584 U.S. 756, 779 (2018).
C.  Lawmakers are accountable to voters for both
action and inaction on assault weapons; courts
are not.
Unlike courts, lawmakers are accountable to voters
who bear the burdens of regulation and the consequences
of gun violence.  That responsibility is especially concrete
for amici Senators Durbin, Blumenthal, and Schiff.
Their constituents include communities in Illinois,
Connecticut, and California that have experienced mass
shootings involving assault weapons firsthand, including
Highland Park, Newtown, and San Bernardino, as well
as communities, including Cook County, that have chosen
to regulate those weapons.  They represent families who
have lost children and loved ones, first responders and lawenforcement officers who confronted the horrors of those

8
attacks, and lawful gun owners, hunters, and sportsmen
with their own stake in the firearms laws enacted by
Congress, the States, and their local governments.
Those constituencies do not necessarily agree on
whether or how assault weapons should be regulated.
Some look to their elected representatives for stronger
measures to prevent another tragedy; others raise
concerns about restrictions on firearms they lawfully own
and use.  Lawmakers must take those competing interests
seriously, make choices that respect constitutional rights
while addressing the concerns of the communities they
serve, and then answer for those choices—to constituents
who supported them and to those who did not, and for
inaction no less than for the laws they enact.
This responsibility to the electorate is a defining
feature of representative government.  Lawmakers must
hear competing views, defend their judgments publicly, and
face voters who may reject them.  The people affected by
firearms policy are not merely subject to those decisions;
they have a continuing voice in who makes them.  That
accountability is among the reasons our constitutional
system entrusts policy choices to legislatures in the first
place.
The Court has recognized the importance of
preserving democratic decision-making on questions the
Constitution leaves unresolved.  As Justice Kavanaugh
explained in Rahimi, the history-and-tradition approach
respects the democratic process because the rights it
does not establish remain available “to be democratically
adopted or rejected by the people.”  602 U.S. at 734
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring) (quoting McDonald v. City of

9
Chicago, 561 U.S. 742, 805 (2010) (Scalia, J., concurring)).
Public policy remains the responsibility of representatives
answerable to the public.
D.  Lawmakers are particularly equipped to
develop the factual record and make predictive
judgments that assault-weapons policy
requires.
Decisions about assault-weapons regulation turn
on difficult empirical and predictive questions—how
particular weapons are used in criminal violence as
compared with lawful uses, what risks their characteristics
present, how manufacturers and consumers may respond
to restrictions, and what effect a given regulatory line is
likely to have.  Legislatures possess institutional tools
particularly suited to investigating these questions.
Through hearings and investigations, testimony from
law enforcement, trauma surgeons, firearms engineers,
criminologists, firearm owners, industry representatives,
and victims of gun violence, and staff expertise developed
over successive sessions, they can assemble a substantial
record, consider competing evidence, and refine legislative
proposals through deliberation and debate.
The breadth of that inquiry distinguishes legislative
policymaking from adjudication.  Courts ordinarily
resolve particular disputes on records developed by the
parties before them.  Legislatures can undertake wider
investigations, examining evidence across jurisdictions
and over time, soliciting perspectives beyond those
represented in any particular litigation, and assessing
the consequences of competing regulatory approaches for
the public as a whole.  No single case record is designed

10
to capture the full range of information lawmakers may
consider in addressing a problem of national scope.
As this Court has recognized, Congress is “far better
equipped than the judiciary to amass and evaluate the
vast amounts of data bearing upon legislative questions.”
Turner Broad. Sys., Inc. v. FCC, 520 U.S. 180, 195 (1997)
(citation modified).
That institutional capacity is especially important
b e ca u s e  fir e arm s  p o li c y  o fte n  r e q uir e s  l a wm ak e rs  to
make prospective judgments in the face of uncertainty.
No legislative record can establish with certainty how a
proposed restriction will operate, whether it will achieve
its intended objectives, or how regulated actors may adapt.
Yet the absence of definitive answers does not relieve
lawmakers of the responsibility to decide whether action
is warranted.  This Court has recognized the “traditional
legislative authority to make predictive judgments when
enacting nationwide regulatory policy.”  Id. at 196.  The
legislative process allows lawmakers to evaluate the
available evidence, consider the likely consequences of
different approaches, and make informed judgments even
where reasonable disagreement remains.
Nor is legislative fact-finding confined to the
record available when a law is enacted.  Legislatures
can continue to investigate how a regulation operates,
assess developments that were not anticipated at the
time of enactment, and incorporate what they learn into
subsequent legislation.  The evaluation of the Federal
Assault Weapons Ban, discussed in Section II.B below,
illustrates the value of that continuing inquiry.  Its
findings concerning both the decline in criminal use of
assault weapons and the effects of grandfathering and

11
substitution provided information relevant to whether
future restrictions should be differently designed.
That capacity is particularly valuable as firearms
technology and patterns of use evolve.  Connecticut’s
experience illustrates the process.  As firearm designs
evolved and experience under the existing framework
developed, its legislature revisited the lines it had drawn,
adjusting definitions and regulatory approaches to account
for new information.  See, e.g., 56 Conn. Gen. Assemb. H.
Procs. at 9245–351 (2013).  Legislatures thus possess not
only the tools to investigate a problem before acting, but
the means to continue learning from their decisions and
respond as circumstances change.
None of this means that legislative judgments
establish constitutionality.  Courts remain responsible
for enforcing the Second Amendment’s limits.  But where
those limits leave policy choices open, disagreement over
how a permissible regulation should be designed, whether
it is optimally effective, or how competing evidence
should be weighed does not, without more, render the
law unconstitutional.  Those judgments call upon the
breadth of inquiry, predictive assessment, and continuing
evaluation that legislative institutions are particularly
equipped to undertake.
II.  CONGRESS’S EXPERIENCE WITH THE
FEDERAL ASSAULT WEAPONS BAN
ILLUSTRATES THE IMPORTANCE OF
PRESERVING LAWMAKER AUTHORITY
Congress’s experience with the Federal Assault
Weapons Ban (the “Ban”) illustrates those institutional

12
strengths in practice.  Congress enacted the Ban after
years of hearings and debate, making deliberate choices
about the scope, operation, and duration of federal
regulation.  The evidence generated while the Ban was
in force then shed light on both its effects—including
declines in the criminal use of assault weapons—and
how its statutory design affected its reach.  Together,
that experience demonstrates the value of a legislative
process in which lawmakers can make difficult policy
judgments, evaluate their consequences, and revisit them
as circumstances change.
A.  Congress enacted the Federal Assault Weapons
Ban through a deliberate legislative process.
Congress’s landmark 1994 assault-weapons legislation
illustrates how lawmakers translate competing evidence
and interests into a regulatory scheme.  Beyond the
threshold question of whether to act, Congress had
to determine which weapons to cover, where to draw
the statutory lines, how to treat existing owners, what
exceptions to recognize, and whether the resulting
restrictions should remain in effect indefinitely.
The Ban imposed a ten-year restriction on the
manufacture, transfer, and possession of specified
semiautomatic assault weapons.  See Public Safety and
Recreational Firearms Use Prot. Act, Pub. L. No. 103-
322, §§ 110101–110106, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996–2010 (1994)
(codified at 18 U.S.C. § 922(v)–(w) (repealed effective 2004)).
Congress acted after extensive hearings over multiple
sessions, receiving testimony from law-enforcement
officials, firearms experts, medical professionals, victims
of gun violence, Second Amendment scholars, and industry

13
representatives.  See, e.g., Assault Weapons: A View from
the Front Lines: Hearing on S. 639 and S. 653 Before the
S. Comm. on the Judiciary , 103d Cong. (1993).
The resulting statute reflected deliberate choices
about the scope of federal regulation.  Congress defined
the regulated category through two approaches: a list
of specifically named models and a set of feature-based
criteria.  The named-model approach identified particular
firearms—including specified AR-15- and AK-47-type
weapons—that Congress sought to regulate.  See 18 U.S.C.
§ 921(a)(30) (1994 repealed effective 2004).  The featurebased approach supplemented that list by identifying
combinations of characteristics, such as pistol grips,
folding or telescoping stocks, flash suppressors, and
bayonet mounts, that placed additional semiautomatic
firearms within the regulated category.  Id.  These
definitions reflected judgments about which weapons and
features warranted restriction, rather than a general
prohibition on semiautomatic firearms.
Congress also made choices about the interests the
legislation would protect.  The statute grandfathered
semiautomatic assault weapons lawfully possessed before
enactment, protecting individuals who had lawfully
acquired regulated firearms, see 18 U.S.C.§ 922(v)(2), and
created exceptions for specified categories of firearms and
government uses, see 18 U.S.C. § 922(v)(3)–(4).  Congress
further included a ten-year sunset provision, requiring
the restrictions to expire on September 13, 2004, unless
Congress affirmatively renewed them.  Pub. L. No.
103-322, § 110105, 108 Stat. at 2000.  These provisions
reflected the compromises that shaped the legislation.
As Senator Patrick Leahy explained during the debate,

14
both Democratic and Republican legislators “influenced
the shape and content of this bill,” including through
amendments accepted in the Senate, the Judiciary
Committee, and conference.  Statement of Sen. Patrick
Leahy, 140 Cong. Rec. 23999 (1994).
The Ban thus reflected more than an initial
determination that federal action was warranted.  Its
provisions embodied legislative compromises over the
reach, operation, and duration of federal regulation—a
policy that could be implemented, studied, and reconsidered
as experience developed.
B.  The Federal Assault Weapons Ban effectively
reduced the criminal use of assault weapons
and mass-shooting deaths.
The Ban’s operation produced substantial evidence
relevant to the policy judgments Congress made in
1994.  A 2004 comprehensive evaluation funded by the
National Institute of Justice (the “Koper Report”) found
that “criminal use of [assault weapons] . . . declined after
1994, independently of trends in gun crime” and that
assault weapons “typically fell by one-third or more as a
share of guns used in crime” in various places and times
from the late 1990s through 2003, with post-2000 data
suggesting reductions as high as 70%.  Christopher S.
Koper, Daniel J. Woods & Jeffrey A. Roth, An Updated
Assessment of the Federal Assault Weapons Ban:
Impacts on Gun Markets and Gun Violence, 1994-2003 ,
51–52 (2004), https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/
abstracts/updated-assessment-federal-assault-weaponsban-impacts-gun-markets  (last accessed Oct. 26, 2026).
Relative to pre-Ban levels, the proportion of gun crimes

15
involving assault weapons dropped by 17% to 72% across
the localities studied.  Id. at 2.
The Koper Report also identified factors that limited
the Ban’s reach: continued circulation of grandfathered
large-capacity magazines manufactured before the Ban;
likely pre-Ban growth in production and marketing of
guns with large-capacity magazines; increased use of nonbanned semiautomatics with large-capacity magazines;
and substitution of post-Ban guns similar to prohibited
assault rifles.  Id. at 52, 65, 79, 96.  These findings helped
reveal how the statute’s definitions and exceptions
operated in practice, and where a different regulatory
design might produce different results.
Subsequent research has associated the Ban with
reductions in mass shootings and deaths.  Comparing
the ten-year periods before, during, and after the Ban,
Professor Louis Klarevas, an expert who testified in both
Viramontes  and Grant at the district court, found that
its implementation coincided with a 37% decline in gun
massacres and a 43% decline in gun-massacre deaths,
while the decade after its expiration saw a 183% increase
in incidents and a 239% increase in deaths.  Declaration of
Professor Louis Klarevas in Support of Defs.’ Opposition
to Motion for Preliminary Injunction at 12–13, Miller
v. Becerra , No. 19-cv-1537-BEN-JLB (S.D. Cal. Jan.
23, 2020), Dkt. No. 33-5.  The pattern persisted after
accounting for population growth.  See id. at 13.
State-level research provides additional evidence.
Professor Klarevas’s analysis of three decades of
data (1990–2019) found that States restricting assault
weapons experienced reductions in gun-massacre

16
incidence and fatalities relative to States without such
restrictions.  Id. at 16–17.  Other studies using different
methodologies have likewise found associations between
assault-weapons restrictions and reductions in public
mass shootings, deaths, or injuries.  See Lori Post, et al.,
Impact of Firearm Surveillance on Gun Control Policy:
Regression Discontinuity Analysis, 7 JMIR Pub. Health
& Surveillance (2021); Mark Gius, The Impact of State
and Federal Assault Weapons Bans on Public Mass
Shootings, 22 Applied Econ. Letters 281 (2014).
The evidence has its limitations.  But this research
provides more than competing assessments of the Ban’s
success: it supplies information about the consequences
of the particular choices Congress made—information
that can inform the scope and design of future legislation.
Congress’s experience with the Ban therefore
illustrates a continuing legislative responsibility.  The
process does not end when a law is enacted: its operation
generates evidence that lawmakers can consider in
deciding whether to maintain, refine, or replace a
regulatory approach.  The value of that experience lies
in Congress’s continuing capacity to act on what it learns.
C.  A categorical rule would improperly foreclose
policy judgments like those Congress made in
enacting the Federal Assault Weapons Ban.
Petitioners contend that AR-15s and similar
semiautomatic rifles cannot be prohibited under the
Second Amendment because there are so many of them.
See Petition for Writ of Certiorari at 25–27, Grant v.
Higgins , No. 25-566 (Nov. 7, 2025) (arguing AR-15s

17
and similar rifles are arms, and arms “in common use”
cannot be banned); Petition for Writ of Certiorari at 26,
Viramontes v. Cook County , No. 25-238 (Aug. 27, 2025)
(same).  That rule would reach far beyond the laws of
Cook County and Connecticut, foreclosing precisely the
kind of policy judgment entrusted to elected lawmakers
and exercised by Congress in enacting the Ban: whether,
after weighing the evidence and the competing concerns
of those it represents, to prohibit specified semiautomatic
assault weapons.  It would not merely reject the particular
judgments those lawmakers made; it would deny Congress,
the States, and local governments the authority to make
that choice at all, regardless of the evidence before them,
the concerns of their constituents, or what experience may
reveal in the years ahead.
Constitutional rights, of course, necessarily constrain
democratic choice.  As Heller recognized, the enshrinement
of a right takes certain policy choices “off the table.”
554 U.S. at 636.  But the distinction between enforcing
a constitutional prohibition and creating one where
the Constitution does not require it is consequential.
Lawmakers’ policy judgments remain subject to political
challenge and revision.  A constitutional ruling that
places a regulatory option beyond legislative authority
cannot be revisited through ordinary lawmaking, however
compelling the evidence or widespread the public demand
for change.  The Court should be especially careful not to
foreclose democratic choice where the Second Amendment
does not compel that result.
That concern is particularly acute where constitutional
protection is said to follow from the prevalence of a
particular weapon in private hands.  A firearm may

18
proliferate before lawmakers have fully assessed its
characteristics, patterns of use, or consequences.  If
widespread ownership alone sufficed to place a weapon
beyond legislative prohibition, the opportunity to regulate
could disappear before legislators had developed the
information necessary to make an informed judgment.  As
the Fourth Circuit observed in Bianchi, such an approach
could “foreclose the ability of legislators to assess
these characteristics and to enhance their knowledge
through observation and experience.”  111 F .4th at 461.
The Constitution should not be understood to require
legislatures to anticipate every danger before it emerges,
on pain of losing the authority to respond once it does.
A categorical rule would also deny different
jurisdictions the ability to reach different conclusions about
a contested question of public safety.  Illinois, Connecticut,
other States, and localities within them have adopted
different approaches to assault-weapons regulation,
reflecting the judgments of their respective legislatures
and electorates.  That variation is not a flaw in our system;
it is an expression of it.  Cf. Gregory v. Ashcroft , 501 U.S.
452, 458 (1991) (recognizing that federalism “allows for
more innovation and experimentation in government”).
Bianchi respected that principle in declining to place
the regulated weapons “beyond the reach of our nation’s
democratic processes” while expressing “no view on
how a state should regulate firearms.”  111 F .4th at 442.
A categorical ruling from this Court would settle the
question for every jurisdiction, leaving no room for the
different policy judgments their elected representatives
might otherwise make.

19
And the consequences would endure.  Weapons
change.  The ways they are manufactured, marketed,
modified, and misused change with them.  Evidence
that supports a regulatory judgment today may be
strengthened, qualified, or displaced by what lawmakers
learn tomorrow.  Congress’s experience with the Federal
Assault Weapons Ban illustrates the importance of
preserving the ability to respond to those developments.
The legislation enacted in 1994 reflected the evidence and
concerns of its time; its operation informed later debates;
and Congress and the States have continued to confront
questions that earlier lawmakers could not have fully
anticipated.  A categorical constitutional rule would not
merely decide what legislatures may do today.  It would
constrain what future generations may do with knowledge
that we do not yet possess.
Amici are not bystanders to this choice.  They
represent the families of Highland Park and Newtown,
other communities that gun violence has affected, lawful
gun owners and sportsmen, law-enforcement officers, and
first responders.  With each election, they are accountable
for the decisions they make.  This is precisely why the
Constitution entrusts permissible policy choices to
representative government.
Behind every assault-weapons statute stands a
legislature that had to make difficult judgments and an
electorate entitled to demand an accounting of them.
Those judgments will not always produce agreement, nor
will every legislative choice prove wise or effective.  But
where the Constitution permits a choice, the people must
remain free to demand a different answer from those they
elect to represent them.

20
Within the Second Amendment’s limits, this Court
should leave the difficult judgments of firearms policy
where our constitutional system places them: with the
elected representatives of Cook County, Illinois, and
Connecticut, answerable to the people they serve, and
with future generations who must confront challenges
that ours cannot yet foresee.  The Constitution protects
the rights of the people.  It also entrusts the people with
the responsibility of governing themselves.  The Court
should preserve both.
CONCLUSION
For all these reasons, the judgments below should be
affirmed.
